doc.title: Jane Monheit interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 20, 2010

title: Producing the new album, Emarcy and managers
summary: Her fifth label, Emarcy, lets her produce a standards album with her band; her managers and father's business management.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: How have things changed for you, getting back to the recordings now, you’re listed as, you’ve got a new one coming out that you’re listed as producer.
So that kind of thing doesn’t happen overnight. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

No it did not. It took ten years, although I co-produced my Christmas album, but it was really time. I’m with a new label now, I’m with Emarcy now. I’ve been in, what is this my fifth label. N-Coded Music, SONY Classical, Epic, Concord and now Emarcy. And a lot of artists change labels frequently. It’s fine you know. I mean you fit in different places at different times in your life and it’s great. And it doesn’t mean anything bad happened at any of those labels, you just, you know, rosters constantly change, and so I’m with Emarcy now. And before I signed with them I knew what record I wanted to make, I went to them — well I didn’t, my manager went to them. Managers, they handle all that stuff. Well some artists do but I don’t really. I’m behind it but I don’t do the day- to-day like making the phone calls and things like that.
Have you been through a number of managers?

Um hum. I’m with Cynthia Herbst at American International Artists right now. I love her. She is an amazing woman. She is the third manager I’ve been with, fourth if you count my dad taking over for a minute.
Yeah I was wondering about that.

Because he business-managed me for a long time. My father is a brilliant, brilliant businessman. And business-managed me for a minute. Because there’s a lot going on. It’s not something I really want to handle myself. There’s a corporation that all of the funds go through, and it’s complicated. For me the personal stuff is enough. I’d rather have the business stuff go through someone who’s got a much better brain for that sort of stuff, and he’s my father, and he did it for a while. But now I’m being business-managed by my management firm. But yeah, I went to Emarcy, or my manager did, and he said this is the record that Jane wants to make. She will produce it and it will be a standards record with her band, harking back to the first albums, going back to my roots big time, and they said all right, great, let’s do it, her way. Awesome. And somebody finally gave me a chance which is great. And that could be for several reasons, you know it could be because I’ve been around for a long time and made a lot of records. I’m sure that’s part of it. It also could be because no one’s really selling a ton of records right now and my moment as like this super hot commodity is over with and now I’m just an established touring artist. I’m sure it’s for a lot of reasons, but whatever it is it was necessary. Because I don’t need anybody to tell me what to do, how to play standards with my band and make a traditional jazz vocal album and tell me how to sing. I don’t need that in my life.
